newsitem.title: INDIA: Tibetans to protest during Jiang's India visit.
newsitem.headline: Tibetans to protest during Jiang's India visit.

text.p: Pro-democracy Tibetan exiles plan to burn the Chinese flag and an effigy of Chinese President Jiang Zemin during his four-day visit to India beginning on Thursday, protest leaders said.

"The police have not given us permission to hold a demonstration in the city so we are holding it at the Tibetan camp in old Delhi," Sonam Chophel, spokesman of the Tibetan Freedom Movement, told Reuters on Wednesday.
Jiang, the first Chinese President to visit India, will arrive in New Delhi on Thursday and will fly to Pakistan on Sunday, Indian foreign ministry officials said.
Chophel said about 600 Tibetans would participate in Thursday's demonstration where they plan to burn 37 Chinese flags and an effigy of Jiang.
"For 37 years Tibet has been ruled by China," he said. "The burning of the Chinese flag symbolises that in 1959 China invaded Tibet."
The Delhi office of the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, said it was not encouraging the demonstrations.

"Officially we have not issued anything. All those doing it are either the Tibetan people or NGOs (non-governmental organisations)," Jampal Chosang, a senior official in the Dalai Lama's office in Delhi, said.
"We ask our people to abide by the rules and regulations of the host country and do whatever they are doing non-violently," he added.
Around 130,000 Tibetans live in India, 4,000 of them in the capital New Delhi.
Chophel said the police made no preventive arrests ahead of Jiang's visit.
India arrested scores of Tibetan protesters in 1991 during a visit by Chinese Premier Li Peng.
Protesters shouting "Death to Li Peng" were seen as a major embarrassment by both governments during his visit.
Chinese officials, saying the Tibetans had threatened to kill Li, cancelled a scheduled visit to the Taj Mahal in Agra and a news conference for security reasons.
But at least 10 Tibetans slipped through police cordons in Delhi and demonstrated in front of the Chinese Embassy before being arrested.

The Dalai Lama fled his homeland along with thousands of followers in 1959 after an abortive uprising against communist rule. Although his government-in-exile is based in northern India, India supports China's jurisdiction over Tibet.
China's premier imposed martial law in the Himalayan region in March 1989 after police crushed pro-independence demonstrations in the capital, Lhasa. It was lifted in May 1990.
